title: Collaborative Evaluation Protocol for Creole Tomatoes in Participatory Breeding Programs
author: Almendra Cremaschi
materials: Define and Prepare Seed Materials Germination test. Credits: Sabrina Rendón Once the trial objectives and the Target Product Profile are defined, select and prepare the tomato accessions for distribution. Source candidate accessions from public germplasm banks, previous participatory evaluation or breeding cycles, or seed-saving networks. Document provenance, multiplication history, and key metadata for each accession to support traceability throughout the trial. Select three (3) tomato accessions that are genetically distinct and representative of the traits prioritized for the current trial cycle. Ensure that the selection reflects both scientific criteria and participants’ preferences defined during the co-design phase. Perform germination tests when feasible to verify seed viability. A local check variety should be included as a reference. This can be either (i) a commonly grown commercial variety or (ii) a locally adapted farmer variety already known to the participant. The inclusion of a local check is optional and context-dependent, and aims to facilitate relative comparison under each participant’s conditions, rather than strict standardization across sites. Ensure sufficient seed quantity to provide each participant with at least 10 seeds per accession, securing a minimum of 6–8 viable plants per accession under typical growing conditions. The protocol does not require within-site replication (e.g., multiple plots per accession per participant). Instead, it follows a participatory and citizen science approach in which each participant represents a single observational unit. In this design, robustness is achieved through the aggregation of observations across a large number of participants and diverse environments, rather than through controlled replication within a single site. This allows the evaluation of varietal performance under real-world growing conditions while maintaining feasibility for non-expert participants (Van Etten et al., 2019). Assign each accession an unambiguous code or name (e.g., “Accession A,” “Accession B,” “Accession C”). Use this naming convention consistently across seed envelopes, the Observation Template, and all communication materials to prevent misidentification and data loss.

Prepare and Distribute Materials Seed Packaging and Labeling of Tomato Accessions (Bioleft). Credits: Karina Schofield Prepare and distribute a complete package to each participant before the recommended planting period. Include the following information on each seed package and envelope: Accession name or code Place of origin Harvest year or seed multiplication date Complete distribution at least 2–3 weeks before the expected sowing date to allow time for soil preparation, planning, and clarification of questions. Distribute seed packages using one or more of the channels below. Track all deliveries to ensure receipt by participants. Use the seed distribution tracking database provided here Seed distribution tracking database.xlsx By mail: Send seed packages using registered post or courier services. Enable tracking and confirm reception with participants. By hand: Deliver seed packages in person during workshops, meetings, or through direct handover. Through local allies: Delegate distribution to trusted community-based organizations or local networks when appropriate. Provide each participant with a digital welcome kit to support implementation and communication throughout the trial. Include the following components: Observation Template (Excel-based): Send the Observation Template electronically (by email or WhatsApp). Ensure that fields are organized by phenological stage and accession. Provide basic guidance on how to complete the template, including where to enter observations and how to save and submit the file. Communication channel invitation: Share a digital invitation to the WhatsApp group or other designated communication channel used for ongoing support, coordination, and sharing of experiences throughout the campaign. Supplementary learning materials: Provide access to visual and written materials that support participants during the growing cycle, such as: Instructional videos (e.g., tutorials on tomato cultivation from seed to harvest, YouTube tutorial on how to grow tomatoes from seed to fruit ) Example cases, including reference photos and completed Observation Templates Ensure that all materials are accessible using commonly available devices and do not require specialized software beyond standard spreadsheet tools. Invite participants to a kick-off webinar or workshop to review the protocol, data sheet, and key observation stages. An example of a kick-off workshop is available here: https://youtu.be/fVAg0whFJ5w?si=_YuVxwdWlYxLZstF

steps.title: Define objectives and TPP
steps.instruction: Through a co‑design workshop (e.g., Bioleft participatory tomato workshop – FAUBA, 2020) collaboratively define the trial purpose (varietal evaluation, participatory selection, conservation) and draft a Target Product Profile (TPP) describing desired agronomic, culinary, cultural and adaptation traits; align selected traits with the Observation Template and adapt the template if new traits are added.

steps.title: Set up on‑farm trial
steps.instruction: Establish the trial under usual cultivation conditions with no standardized plot size; apply identical management practices to all accessions and avoid any special treatment; complete all required trial metadata fields as indicated in the protocol.

steps.title: Recruit and onboard participants
steps.instruction: Select agroecological producers, family farmers and gardeners interested in heirloom tomatoes, prioritizing commitment to grow three accessions, record observations, and engage in peer learning; aim for a balanced cohort of roughly 30–40 participants across regions, genders and growing contexts; disseminate an open call via social media and networks, collect applications through a digital sign‑up form, obtain signed participation‑commitment forms, and note that historically only about 15 % of recruited participants complete the full observation cycle.

steps.title: Sow seeds and record conditions
steps.instruction: Sow each accession separately in seedbeds, nurseries or containers, labeling all containers, trays and seedlings at every step; record day temperature (ideally 21–27 °C), night temperature (ideally 13–18 °C) and relative humidity (ideally 60–80 %) at sowing; consider staggered sowing by planting half of the seeds now and the remaining half 10–15 days later to reduce climatic risk; maintain clear accession identification throughout emergence and record sowing/emergence data in the Observation Template.

steps.title: Transplant seedlings to final location
steps.instruction: When seedlings have at least two fully expanded leaves, transplant them to their final growing location—either containers or directly into soil—recording the transplant date in the Observation Template; adjust timing to avoid frost or very low temperatures; note whether the transplant is to containers or soil as required by the spreadsheet.

steps.title: Apply routine crop management
steps.instruction: Carry out all usual crop‑management practices (e.g., irrigation, fertilization, pest control) throughout the tomato cycle, repeating them as needed; record the date(s) and, when applicable, the frequency of each practice for each accession in the Observation Template; include pruning events and any other management actions.

steps.title: Monitor growth and disease symptoms
steps.instruction: Observe plant growth, phenological stage, stress responses, health and uniformity after transplant; record any plant death due to pests or diseases; if relevant, include priority diseases such as Tomato brown rugose fruit virus or bacterial wilt, using provided visual guides (e.g., Bioleft ToBRFV guide); when disease identification is uncertain, describe symptoms rather than assign a formal diagnosis; enter all observations in the Observation Template.

steps.title: Document fruiting‑stage practices
steps.instruction: During fruit set to harvest, note any optional management practices applied (e.g., vigor control, fruit‑development treatments); for each practice record the date and a brief description in the Observation Template.

steps.title: Harvest and record post‑harvest data
steps.instruction: Harvest fruits when they reach eating maturity (typically near‑full coloration) according to local preference; record harvest dates, yield estimates and post‑harvest duration in days; if fruits are stored refrigerated, specify the storage condition and record both ambient and refrigerated post‑harvest durations in the Observation Template.

steps.title: Consolidate data and generate report
steps.instruction: Collect all completed Observation Templates from participants, clean, harmonize and validate the data in a centralized database; use the automatically generated fields from the final sheet for aggregation while preserving traceability; produce a collective results report summarizing agronomic, sensory and experiential findings; organize a feedback workshop where results are presented to participants, breeders, researchers and partners; optionally record the workshop (e.g., https://youtu.be/Xhrdqwst1u0).

steps.title: Conduct sensory evaluation
steps.instruction: Perform two complementary sensory assessments: (1) participant‑based evaluation where all trial participants rate flavor, texture, aroma and overall appreciation of their own tomatoes using a 9‑point hedonic scale (1 = dislike very much, 5 = neutral, 9 = like very much); (2) consumer‑based collective tasting events with a recommended minimum of 20–30 external evaluators (more if feasible) following the same 9‑point scale; integrate both data sets in the collective analysis phase.
